L2686@P32: Once the user is ready for the latest version of the asset to be exported again, the
L2687@P32: asset is unbranched (Figure 8).
L2688@P32: Asset types were added to allow the
L2689@P32: teams to classify new assets added to the
L2690@P32: system. Some of these asset types, such as
L2691@P32: “Mesh (in game)” or “Texture (in game)”
L2692@P32: are backed by code in the asset manager
L2693@P32: that performs special functions. In these
L2694@P32: two cases, in-game versions of the assets
L2695@P32: are created and checked in whenever the
L2696@P32: original assets themselves are checked in.
L2697@P32: Future Work
L2698@P32: While our asset management system
L2699@P32: has solved a number of problems
L2700@P32: that we have experienced in managing
L2701@P32: game assets in the past, several areas still
L2702@P32: need additional work. The hardest area
L2703@P32: that we have yet to address is the issue of
L2704@P32: the “build machine” — the versioning of
L2705@P32: the tools themselves. We’ve already run
L2706@P32: into this problem once in creating a patch
L2707@P32: for one of our previous games almost a
L2708@P32: year after it shipped. The original game
L2709@P32: was compiled using Microsoft Visual C++
L2710@P32: 5. Our current compiler is Visual C++ 6
L2711@P32: with Service Pack 3.
L2712@P32: Getting the game to finally compile correctly with the latest version of the compiler took several days. While the new compiler certainly improved the code quality
L2713@P32: and allowed us to find some problems that
L2714@P32: the old compiler had missed, we don’t
L2715@P32: know what additional problems the new
L2716@P32: compiler might have introduced.
L2717@P32: It seems that the only way to fully version-off the tools that were used to create
L2718@P32: the game is to set a workstation in the corner that contains the tools and the shipping version of the source code. Any other
L2719@P32: solution that involves storing the program
L2720@P32: install disks away and having to reinstall
L2721@P32: old software probably will not be utilized.
L2722@P32: One of the other problems to solve is
L2723@P32: being able to regenerate all the in-game
L2724@P32: versions of assets from the original versions stored in the asset manager.
L2725@P32: Although we try to make sure that we
L2726@P32: never break existing game assets, there
L2727@P32: usually comes a time (sometimes more
L2728@P32: than once, unfortunately) where all of the
L2729@P32: art, sound, or levels for the game need to
L2730@P32: be reprocessed. With the original data, and
L2731@P32: the information on how it was exported
L2732@P32: for the game stored in the asset manager,
L2733@P32: it’s possible to write a batch system that
L2734@P32: can perform this reconversion. One of our
L2735@P32: next goals is to actually implement this
L2736@P32: using the Max DCOM sample code to create our own batch system to reprocess
L2737@P32: assets as necessary.
L2738@P32: Summary
L2739@P32: I
L2740@P32: n the end, it would have been easier if
L2741@P32: there were an off-the-shelf asset management solution that met our needs right
L2742@P32: out of the box. Those asset management
L2743@P32: systems directed towards game and content creation all seem competent in delivering basic asset management functionality, but they are sorely lacking in the areas
L2744@P32: of front-end and third-party integration
L2745@P32: and workflow.
L2746@P32: For us, developing an asset management
L2747@P32: system completely in-house was well
L2748@P32: worth the effort. We ended up with a system that met our needs, and because we
L2749@P32: fully understand the design and architecture, we can continue to add functionality
L2750@P32: as needs arise.
L2751@P32: The total staffing time was about eight
L2752@P32: full-time man-weeks of programming, and
L2753@P32: three part-time weeks of testing. The programming time did run over by a couple of
L2754@P32: weeks, but this was mainly due to adding
L2755@P32: new features during development. It
L2756@P32: should also be noted that the programming time would have taken significantly
L2757@P32: longer if we hadn’t already had back-end
L2758@P32: server design and implementation experience in-house.
L2759@P32: Overall, the biggest problems revolved
L2760@P32: around our inability to modify and integrate with the Max user interface system
L2761@P32: more simply. The whole Max user interface needs to be based on MaxScript, and
L2762@P32: MaxScript itself needs to be much more
L2763@P32: powerful in order to do what we need to
L2764@P32: do. An even better solution would be if
L2765@P32: Max provided a specified asset management interface similar to Microsoft’s Visual
L2766@P32: C++, thereby allowing third parties to create asset management solutions for it. q

L2798@P32: ASSET MANAGEMENT
L2799@P32-33: ACKNOWLEDGEMENTSFictionally, DEUS EX is set in a
L2800@P33: near-future version of the real
L2801@P33: world (as it exists if conspiracy buffs are right). For some
L2802@P33: real shorthand, call it “James
L2803@P33: Bond meets The X-Files.”
L2804@P33: Conceptually, DEUS EX is a genre-busting game (which really endeared us to the
L2805@P33: marketing guys) — part immersive simulation, part role-playing game, part first-person shooter, part adventure game. It’s an
L2806@P33: immersive simulation game in that you are
L2807@P33: made to feel you’re actually in the game
L2808@P33: world with as little as possible getting in
L2809@P33: the way of the experience of “being there.”
L2810@P33: Ideally, nothing reminds you that you’re
L2811@P33: just playing a game — not interface, not
L2812@P33: your character’s back-story or capabilities,
L2813@P33: not game systems, nothing. It’s all about
L2814@P33: how you interact with a relatively complex
L2815@P33: environment in ways that you find interesting (rather than in ways the developers
L2816@P33: think are interesting), and in ways that
L2817@P33: move you closer to accomplishing your
L2818@P33: goals (not the developers’ goals).
L2819@P33: It’s also a role-playing game in that you
L2820@P33: play a role and make character development choices that ensure that you end up
L2821@P33: with a unique alter ego. You make your
L2822@P33: way through a variety of minute-to-minute
L2823@P33: gameplay experiences (which add up to a
L2824@P33: story) in a manner that grows naturally
L2825@P33: out of the unique aspects of your character. Every game system is designed to differentiate one player-character from another, and to allow players to make decisions
L2826@P33: that reflect their own biases and express
L2827@P33: character differences in obvious ways in
L2828@P33: the game world.
L2829@P33: It’s a first-person shooter because the
L2830@P33: action unfolds in real time, seen through the
L2831@P33: virtual eyes of your alter ego in the game
L2832@P33: world. To some extent, your reflexes and
L2833@P33: skill determine your success in combat.
L2834@P33: However, unlike the typical FPS, DEUS EX
L2835@P33: doesn’t force you to shoot every virtual
L2836@P33: thing that moves. Also unlike the average
L2837@P33: FPS, in which gameplay is limited to pulling
L2838@P33: a virtual trigger, finding blue keys to open
L2839@P33: blue doors, and jumping to reach seemingly
L2840@P33: inaccessible locations, DEUS EX offers players a wide range of gameplay options.
L2841@P33: And finally, DEUS EX is like adventure
L2842@P33: games in that it’s story-driven, linear in
L2843@P33: narrative structure, and involves character
L2844@P33: interaction and item accumulation to
L2845@P33: advance the plot. However, unlike most
L2846@P33: adventure games (in which you spend the
L2847@P33: bulk of your time solving clever puzzles in
L2848@P33: a search for the next static, but very pretty,
L2849@P33: screen), DEUS EX asks players to determine
L2850@P33: how they will solve game problems and
L2851@P33: forces them to deal with the consequences
L2852@P33: of their choices.
L2853@P33: DEUS EX combines elements of all of
L2854@P33: these genres. But more important than any
L2855@P33: genre classification, the game was conceived with the idea that we’d accept players as our collaborators, that we’d put
L2856@P33: power back in their hands, ask them to
L2857@P33: make choices, and let them deal with the
L2858@P33: consequences. It was designed from the
L2859@P33: start as a game about player expression,
L2860@P33: not about how clever we are as designers,
L2861@P33: programmers, artists, or storytellers.
L2862@P33: Which leads naturally to a discussion of
L2863@P33: having clear goals — the first thing I think
L2864@P33: we did right.

L2898@P35: 1.A clear high-level vision. It’s
L2899@P35: pretty self-evident that you can’t
L2900@P35: achieve goals if you’re not clear about
L2901@P35: what they are. We knew with a high degree
L2902@P35: of confidence what kind of game we wanted to make. This was possible for two reasons. First, DEUS EX is a natural outgrowth
L2903@P35: of work done by and in some cases with
L2904@P35: the late, lamented Looking Glass Technologies. We were inspired as well by games
L2905@P35: made at Valve, Origin, and a host of other
L2906@P35: places. Many of the things we wanted to
L2907@P35: do were a reaction to things they (or we)
L2908@P35: didn’t do, didn’t do well, or couldn’t do at
L2909@P35: all in earlier games. We weren’t building
L2910@P35: from scratch, but rather building on a
L2911@P35: foundation already laid for us.
L2912@P35: Second, and on a personal level, DEUS EX is a
L2913@P35: game I’ve been thinking
L2914@P35: about since right around the
L2915@P35: time UNDERWORLD 2
L2916@P35: shipped. I’ve tried to get a
L2917@P35: game like this started several times (as TROUBLESHOOTER at Origin; in
L2918@P35: some respects, as
L2919@P35: JUNCTION POINT, for
L2920@P35: Looking Glass). Those
L2921@P35: games didn’t happen for
L2922@P35: a variety of reasons,
L2923@P35: but I never stopped
L2924@P35: thinking about them
L2925@P35: and, despite the failure
L2926@P35: of those games to reach
L2927@P35: production, they laid
L2928@P35: much of the conceptual
L2929@P35: groundwork for DEUS
L2930@P35: EX. The lesson here is
L2931@P35: that if there’s a game you
L2932@P35: really want to make,
L2933@P35: don’t give up on it.
L2934@P35: Someone will be foolish
L2935@P35: enough to give you the
L2936@P35: money eventually.
L2937@P35: Several years passed. I
L2938@P35: left Origin to go work
L2939@P35: for Looking Glass, but
L2940@P35: TROUBLESHOOTER stayed
L2941@P35: on my mind. In the fall of 1997,
L2942@P35: before Ion Storm entered the
L2943@P35: DEUS EX picture, I drafted a manifesto — a
L2944@P35: description of an ideal
L2945@P35: game — and also a
L2946@P35: set of “rules of roleplaying.” Much of
L2947@P35: that material ended
L2948@P35: up in an article published in Game
L2949@P35: Developer (“Remodeling RPGs for the
L2950@P35: New Millennium,”
L2951@P35: February 1999),
L2952@P35: which is still available online on
L2953@P35: Gamasutra.com.
L2954@P35: The details of
L2955@P35: DEUS EX — plot,
L2956@P35: character lists, game
L2957@P35: system designs and so
L2958@P35: on — changed radically in the years
L2959@P35: following the original TROUBLESHOOTER proposal and writing my manifesto and rules list. Conceptually, however, the game still plays much the way
L2960@P35: I hoped TROUBLESHOOTER would
L2961@P35: play, and it definitely fulfills
L2962@P35: most of the ideals I had outlined in that Game Developer article. Quite simply,
L2963@P35: with a solid concept of
L2964@P35: what we wanted to achieve
L2965@P35: in mind, we were able to
L2966@P35: assess every design decision and every game system
L2967@P35: specification in light of our
L2968@P35: ultimate goals.
L2969@P35: 2. We didn’t skimp onpreproduction. We
L2970@P35: spent the first six months of
L2971@P35: DEUS EX (before we licensed a
L2972@P35: game engine), with a team of
L2973@P35: about six, just thinking about
L2974@P35: how we could turn our highlevel goals into a game. We
L2975@P35: hammered on the setting and
L2976@P35: decided to move the game
L2977@P35: into the near future to buy
L2978@P35: ourselves some room to
L2979@P35: play around — the real
L2980@P35: world, as we quickly
L2981@P35: discovered, was very
L2982@P35: limiting. Ultimately,
L2983@P35: we settled on a conspiracy-oriented
L2984@P35: background.
L2985@P35: We did a vast amount of research into
L2986@P35: “real” conspiracies — the Kennedy assassination, Area 51, the CIA pushing crack
L2987@P35: in East L.A., Dwight Eisenhower’s UFO
L2988@P35: connection, and of course Freemasons tunneling below the Denver airport and building abducted-baby cafeterias for alien
L2989@P35: invaders at George Bush’s direction. Only
L2990@P35: a fraction of this stuff ended up in the
L2991@P35: game, but it gave us a peek into the minds
L2992@P35: of conspiracy buffs that was both scary
L2993@P35: and useful.
L2994@P35: We worked on back-story stuff so we’d
L2995@P35: know what was going on in the world,
L2996@P35: even in places the player never got to visit.
L2997@P35: Some of this stuff may come to the forefront in DEUS EX 2 but, for DEUS EX, it was
L2998@P35: just a way of making sure we knew enough
L2999@P35: to include the kinds of small details that
L3000@P35: make a fictional world convincing.
L3001@P35: We also created a cast of more than 200
L3002@P35: characters, many of whom didn’t yet have
L3003@P35: specific roles in the game. Ultimately, this
L3004@P35: list proved to be both a help and a hindrance to designers as they fleshed out the
L3005@P35: missions. Characters sometimes suggested
L3006@P35: missions or subquests, but just as often
L3007@P35: ended up being filler we were reluctant to
L3008@P35: cut, even though their missions or story
L3009@P35: purposes changed during our storylinefocusing passes.
L3010@P35: We hammered on game systems. We
L3011@P35: conceived a skill system that didn’t depend
L3012@P35: on die-rolls or tracking skills at a fine level
L3013@P35: of granularity. We came up with a system

L3016@P35: ABOVE. Real-world spaces, such as the Statue of Liberty in New York
L3017@P35: City, can be compelling game spaces, but offer unique challenges to

L3019@P36: conversation system with some cinematic
L3020@P36: elements and some elements borrowed
L3021@P36: from console RPGs. We mocked up 2D
L3022@P36: inventory, skill, and augmentation upgrade
L3023@P36: screens, map screens, even a text editor so

L3025@P36: several player reward systems, including
L3026@P36: skill point awards, augmentation upgrades,
L3027@P36: weapon availability timelines and tool/-
L3028@P36: object availability timelines.
L3029@P36: By March 1998, we had 300 pages of
L3030@P36: documentation and thought we knew
L3031@P36: everything we’d needed to know to make a
L3032@P36: game. Were we ever wrong. In the time
L3033@P36: between March 1998 and our Alpha 1
L3034@P36: deadline of April 1999, that 300-page document mushroomed into more than 500
L3035@P36: pages, much of it radically different from
L3036@P36: what we thought of and wrote initially.
L3037@P36: Clear goals and a detailed script are all
L3038@P36: well and good, but goals change, thinking
L3039@P36: changes, and game designs have to change,
L3040@P36: too. Which leads nicely into the next thing
